segments.title: HMS Polyanthus in Q-ship guise
segments.summary: An introduction to HMS Polyanthus as an Aubrietia-class Flower sloop shown in her disguised Q-ship form.
segments.body: HMS Polyanthus appears in her Q-ship form as an Aubrietia-class sloop within the wider Flower family. Her outward appearance is part of the story because the disguise made a purpose-built naval vessel look like an ordinary commercial ship. The deception concealed the ship's naval structure and fighting power. This opening prepares the viewer for the later explanation of how minesweeper construction and hidden weapons made Polyanthus dangerous to submarines.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies HMS Polyanthus, her Aubrietia-class sloop type, and Q-ship form.

segments.title: A simple minesweeper built to survive a blast
segments.summary: The Flower sloops combined a straightforward single-screw, triple-expansion layout with protection intended to limit mine damage.
segments.body: The Flower sloops began as simple, straightforward minesweepers. A single screw and triple-expansion engines provided an uncomplicated machinery arrangement suited to that basic role. Three hull layers around the bow were intended to absorb a mine explosion progressively instead of allowing one blast to open the entire forward structure. Keeping the magazines aft also separated the ship's explosives from the area most likely to strike a mine, linking internal arrangement directly to survivability.

evidence.note: The transcript explains the basic minesweeper role, machinery, multiple forward hulls, and aft magazines.

segments.title: From convoy sloop to disguised submarine trap
segments.summary: Reclassified as convoy sloops, these Flower vessels could masquerade as small merchant ships and serve as successful Q-ships.
segments.body: The type changed from minesweeper to convoy sloop and then to Q-ship. Its small merchant-vessel appearance allowed a warship to look like an inviting civilian target. A submarine approaching on that assumption could discover that the apparently harmless ship was built and armed for naval service. An existing hull type could therefore acquire a new anti-submarine role through reclassification and deception rather than an entirely new design.

evidence.note: The transcript covers convoy-sloop reclassification, merchant-ship appearance, Q-ship conversion, and their success in that role.

segments.title: Saxifrage survives as HMS President
segments.summary: Saxifrage's survival into RNVR service as HMS President traces the First World War sloop type into a much later training role.
segments.body: Saxifrage survived long after her Q-ship service. Renamed HMS President in 1922, she became the drill ship for the London Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve unit. She remained in that role until 1988, far beyond the wartime conditions for which the vessel had been built. Her later return to the Saxifrage name and restoration connect the class's operational history with naval training and preservation.

evidence.note: The transcript traces Saxifrage's renaming as HMS President, service as the London RNVR drill ship until 1988, and restoration under her original name.

segments.title: Speed and the limits of coal endurance
segments.summary: Strong construction and better-than-designed speed gave the sloops useful performance, while a 205-ton coal load constrained their range.
segments.body: The ships were exceptionally strongly built and designed for about 17.5 knots. They could often exceed that speed, so their merchant-like appearance understated their performance as well as their strength. Their 205-ton coal capacity nevertheless imposed a practical limit on endurance. The combination suited a robust, reasonably quick escort or submarine hunter, although the vessel was not intended for long-range cruising.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the ships as exceptionally strong, gives their designed and observed speed, and links the 205-ton coal load to limited range.

segments.title: Guns and depth charges behind the disguise
segments.summary: Two 4-inch Mark IV guns, 3-pounder guns, and depth charges turned the merchant-looking sloop into an anti-submarine surprise.
segments.body: The Flower sloops often carried two 4-inch Mark IV guns, 3-pounder guns, and depth charges. That armament was substantial for a vessel presenting itself as a modest merchant ship. The Q-ship method depended on keeping this fighting power from shaping an obviously naval silhouette until a submarine had committed itself. The weapons and merchant disguise served the same anti-submarine purpose: catching an attacker by surprise.

evidence.note: The transcript lists two 4-inch Mark IV guns, smaller guns, and depth charges, then characterizes the vessels as surprises.

segments.title: Why a small merchant-ship silhouette mattered
segments.summary: At 1,250 tons and dressed as a small merchant vessel, a Flower Q-ship could look like an unthreatening target to a submarine.
segments.body: The sloop combined a strong naval hull with a misleading civilian silhouette. At 1,250 tons, she was substantial but could still resemble a very small, ordinary merchant ship. That appearance encouraged a hunting submarine to read her as a target rather than as an armed threat. Even the unusual paint scheme shown in the video gave little warning of the naval structure and weapons behind the disguise.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the ships' strength, 1,250-ton displacement, merchant appearance, and deceptive paint.
